arml-1999-power-01a.title: Solution
arml-1999-power-01a.body:
Here $p(j)=j$, so $p(j)>p(k)$ never happens for $j<k$. Hence $T=\varnothing$ and $N=0$.

**Answer: $T=\varnothing$, $N=0$**

arml-1999-power-01b.title: List the inversions
arml-1999-power-01b.body:
Here $p=3,1,4,5,9,2,6,8,7$. For each position, list later positions with a smaller value: position $1$ (value $3$): positions $2$ ($1$) and $6$ ($2$); position $3$ (value $4$): position $6$; position $4$ (value $5$): position $6$; position $5$ (value $9$): positions $6,7,8,9$; position $8$ (value $8$): position $9$. Others have none.

$T=\{(1,2),(1,6),(3,6),(4,6),(5,6),(5,7),(5,8),(5,9),(8,9)\}$ and $N=9$.

**Answer: $N=9$ with $T$ as above**

arml-1999-power-01c.title: Solution
arml-1999-power-01c.body:
The first $n$ entries are $1,\dots,n$ in increasing order, all smaller than every later entry, so they take part in no turnabout pair. The last $n$ entries $2n,2n-1,\dots,n+1$ are in decreasing order, so every pair of positions among $n+1,\dots,2n$ is in $T$.

$T=\{(j,k): n+1\le j<k\le2n\}$ and $N=\binom n2=\frac{n(n-1)}2$.

**Answer: $N=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$**

arml-1999-power-02a.title: Swap neighbours
arml-1999-power-02a.body:
Swapping two adjacent entries of $1\,2\,3\,4\,5$ creates exactly one out-of-order pair. For example $1\,2\,3\,5\,4$ has $T=\{(4,5)\}$, so $N=1$.

**Answer: e.g. $1\,2\,3\,5\,4$**

arml-1999-power-02b.title: Almost reversed
arml-1999-power-02b.body:
The reversed permutation $6\,5\,4\,3\,2\,1$ has all $\binom62=15$ pairs in $T$. Swapping the last two entries gives $6\,5\,4\,3\,1\,2$, where only the pair $(5,6)$ is in order, so $N=15-1=14$.

**Answer: e.g. $6\,5\,4\,3\,1\,2$**

arml-1999-power-02c.title: Reuse part (b)
arml-1999-power-02c.body:
Append $7,8$ to the permutation $6\,5\,4\,3\,1\,2$ from part (b): $6\,5\,4\,3\,1\,2\,7\,8$. The new entries are larger than all previous ones and in increasing order, so they add no turnabout pairs: $N=14$. (Another example: $1\,2\,8\,7\,6\,5\,3\,4$, where $8\,7\,6\,5\,3\,4$ is the permutation from part (b) shifted up by $2$ and the leading $1,2$ add nothing.)

**Answer: e.g. $6\,5\,4\,3\,1\,2\,7\,8$**

arml-1999-power-02d.title: Almost reversed block
arml-1999-power-02d.body:
The reversed permutation of $1,\dots,9$ has $\binom92=36$ pairs in $T$; swapping its last two entries gives $9\,8\,7\,6\,5\,4\,3\,1\,2$ with $N=35$. Appending $10$ adds nothing: $9\,8\,7\,6\,5\,4\,3\,1\,2\,10$ has $N=35$. (Another: $10\,9\,8\,7\,6\,1\,2\,3\,4\,5$: the five largest entries give $\binom52=10$ pairs among themselves and $5\cdot5=25$ pairs with the five small entries, $35$ in all.)

**Answer: e.g. $9\,8\,7\,6\,5\,4\,3\,1\,2\,10$**

arml-1999-power-03a.title: Construct and check
arml-1999-power-03a.body:
Take $p=4\,1\,5\,2\,6\,3$. Then $p(1)=4$ exceeds the later values $1,2,3$ (positions $2,4,6$) but not $5,6$ (positions $3,5$), giving $(1,2),(1,4),(1,6)$; $p(3)=5$ exceeds $2,3$ (positions $4,6$): $(3,4),(3,6)$; $p(5)=6$ exceeds $3$: $(5,6)$. Entries at even positions ($1,2,3$) are increasing, so no pair $(e,\cdot)$ appears. So $T$ is exactly the set of pairs (odd, even), $T=\{(1,2),(1,4),(1,6),(3,4),(3,6),(5,6)\}$.

**Answer: $4\,1\,5\,2\,6\,3$**

arml-1999-power-03b.title: Reverse each block
arml-1999-power-03b.body:
The pairs required are exactly the pairs of positions that lie in the same block $\{1,\dots,9\}$, $\{10,\dots,19\}$, $\dots$, $\{90,\dots,99\}$ (same tens digit $a$). Take the permutation that lists the blocks in increasing order but each block in decreasing order: $9\,8\,7\cdots1,\ 19\,18\cdots10,\ 29\cdots20,\ \dots,\ 99\,98\cdots90$.

Within a block the order is reversed, so every pair of positions in the block is in $T$; between different blocks the earlier block has smaller values, so no such pair is in $T$. Hence $T$ is as required.

**Answer: $9\,8\cdots1\;19\cdots10\;\cdots\;99\cdots90$**

arml-1999-power-03c.title: Contradiction from three positions
arml-1999-power-03c.body:
Suppose $p=a\,b\,c\cdots$ were such a permutation (so $a=p(1)$, $b=p(2)$, $c=p(3)$). The pair $(1,3)$ has the same parity, so it is in $T$: $a>c$. But $(1,2)$ and $(2,3)$ have different parities, so they are not in $T$: $a<b$ and $b<c$. Then $a<b<c$ contradicts $a>c$.

So no such permutation exists. ∎

arml-1999-power-04.title: Reverse the values
arml-1999-power-04.body:
Let $p$ have turnabout set $T$ and define $q(x)=n+1-p(x)$. Since $p$ is a bijection of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, so is $q$. For a pair $(j,k)$ (so $j<k$) we have $p(j)\ne p(k)$, hence

$(j,k)\in T(q)\iff q(j)>q(k)\iff p(j)<p(k)\iff (j,k)\notin T(p).$

So $T(q)=\overline T$, and the answer is yes. ∎

arml-1999-power-05.title: Recover $p$ from $T$
arml-1999-power-05.body:
Fix $k$ and let $m=p(k)$. Then exactly $m-1$ positions $\ell$ have $p(\ell)<p(k)$. Split them into those with $\ell<k$ and those with $\ell>k$:

- positions $\ell>k$ with $p(\ell)<p(k)$ are exactly those with $(k,\ell)\in T$; let there be $a_k$ of them;
- positions $\ell<k$ with $p(\ell)<p(k)$ are the $\ell<k$ for which $(\ell,k)\notin T$; there are $(k-1)-b_k$ of them, where $b_k=\#\{\ell:(\ell,k)\in T\}$.

Therefore $m-1=a_k+(k-1)-b_k$, i.e. $p(k)=k+a_k-b_k$. The numbers $a_k,b_k$ depend only on $T$, so $T$ determines $p(k)$ for every $k$, hence determines $p$. Two permutations with the same turnabout set are therefore equal. ∎

arml-1999-power-06.title: Induction
arml-1999-power-06.body:
For $n=1$ the only permutation has $N=0=\frac{1\cdot0}2$. Suppose the claim holds for $n-1$: every $t$ with $0\le t\le\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}2$ is the turnabout number of some permutation of $\{1,\dots,n-1\}$. Appending the largest entry $n$ at the right end adds no turnabout pair, so those same values of $t$ occur for $n$.

Now start from $q_0=(n-1)\,(n-2)\cdots1\,n$, with $N=\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}2$. Move $n$ one place to the left at a time: $q_1=(n-1)\cdots2\,n\,1$, $q_2=(n-1)\cdots n\,2\,1$, and so on up to $q_{n-1}=n\,(n-1)\cdots1$. Because $n$ is larger than every entry it passes, each step adds exactly one new turnabout pair, so $N(q_i)=\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}2+i$ and $N(q_{n-1})=\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}2+(n-1)=\frac{n(n-1)}2$.

Thus every $t$ in $\left[0,\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}2\right]$ and every $t$ in $\left[\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}2,\frac{n(n-1)}2\right]$ is achieved, which completes the induction. ∎

arml-1999-power-07b.title: Count smaller values
arml-1999-power-07b.body:
Let $m=p(k)$. Then exactly $m-1$ positions $\ell$ have $p(\ell)<p(k)$. Of the $k-1$ positions $\ell<k$, those with $p(\ell)>p(k)$ are the ones with $(\ell,k)\in T$; let there be $b$ of them, so $k-1-b$ positions $\ell<k$ have $p(\ell)<p(k)$. Of the positions $\ell>k$, those with $p(\ell)<p(k)$ are those with $(k,\ell)\in T$; let there be $a$ of them.

Then $m-1=(k-1-b)+a$, so $p(k)=k+a-b$. ∎

arml-1999-power-08b.title: Example
arml-1999-power-08b.body:
Take $p_1=1\,2\,3\,4$ and $p_2=1\,2\,3\,4$ (turnabout sets empty) and $p_3=4\,1\,2\,3$ with $T(p_3)=\{(1,2),(1,3),(1,4)\}$. No pair is in more than one turnabout set (indeed only $p_3$ has any).

Then $P=(1+1+4,\ 2+2+1,\ 3+3+2,\ 4+4+3)=6\,5\,8\,11$, and $T(P)=\{(1,2)\}$, so $N(P)=1>0$. This shows that it is necessary that every pair be in a turnabout set (the condition that you disagree with exactly one judge on each pair).

**Answer: e.g. $1234,\ 1234,\ 4123$**

arml-1999-power-09.title: Use the formula
arml-1999-power-09.body:
By the formula, for each $m$: $p_m(k)=k+a_k^{(m)}-b_k^{(m)}$ where $a_k^{(m)}$ and $b_k^{(m)}$ count the pairs of $T(p_m)$ starting and ending at $k$. Adding over $m=1,2,3$:

$P(k)=3k+A_k-B_k$, where $A_k$ = number of pairs $(k,j)$ lying in some $T(p_m)$ and $B_k$ = number of pairs $(j,k)$ lying in some $T(p_m)$ (counted with multiplicity, but each pair is counted exactly once).

Every pair of $\{1,2,3,4\}$ occurs exactly once, so $A_k=4-k$ (pairs $(k,j)$ with $j>k$) and $B_k=k-1$ (pairs $(j,k)$ with $j<k$). Hence $P(k)=3k+(4-k)-(k-1)=k+5$, i.e. $P=6\,7\,8\,9$.

$P$ is strictly increasing, so no pair has $P(j)>P(k)$ and $T(P)=\varnothing$. ∎

arml-1999-power-10.title: General formula
arml-1999-power-10.body:
By the formula $p_i(k)=k+a_k^{(i)}-b_k^{(i)}$, summing over $i$: $P(k)=mk+A_k-B_k$, where $A_k$ is the total number of times a pair $(k,j)$ occurs in the turnabout sets and $B_k$ the total number of times a pair $(j,k)$ occurs. Since each pair occurs exactly $\ell$ times, and there are $n-k$ pairs starting at $k$ and $k-1$ pairs ending at $k$: $A_k=\ell(n-k)$, $B_k=\ell(k-1)$.

So $P(k)=mk+\ell(n-k)-\ell(k-1)=mk+\ell(n-2k+1)$. Then $P(k+1)-P(k)=m-2\ell$ for every $k$.

If $m>2\ell$ then $P$ is strictly increasing, and if $m=2\ell$ then $P$ is constant: in both cases no pair has $P(j)>P(k)$, so $T(P)=\varnothing$. If $m<2\ell$ then $P$ is strictly decreasing and every pair is in $T(P)$.

Special cases: $n=4$, $m=3$, $\ell=1$ gives $P(k)=3k+5-2k=k+5$ (problem 9); more generally $m=n-1$ permutations covering each pair once give $P(k)=(n-3)k+n+1$, increasing for $n\ge4$. In the judging context: if each pair is reversed by fewer than half of the $m$ judges ($\ell<m/2$ judges disagree with you on each pair), then the sum of the rankings agrees with your ranking. ∎
